newsitem.title: TAIWAN: C.bank calls Taiwan dollar depreciation normal.
newsitem.headline: C.bank calls Taiwan dollar depreciation normal.

text.p: Taiwan's central bank vowed anew to respect market forces in the foreign exchange trade, saying the Taiwan dollar's slide through a key defence threshold on Tuesday reflected only the U.S. dollar's strength.

The Taiwan dollar sank to its lowest close in more than eight years against the U.S. currency on Tuesday after the central bank abandoned its longtime defence of T$28 to the U.S. dollar. The rate ended at T$28.17.
The central bank, in a statement issued after the close of trading, said the currency's fall reflected normal trade and that the magnitude of its long slide since 1996 was not great.

"The U.S. dollar has remained strong against all currencies recently, and today's T$28.170 close represented a depreciation of only 2.41 percent from the end of last year," the central bank statement said.
"The recent Taiwan dollar depreciation reflects only the U.S. dollar's strength. Market trading is normal," the bank said.
"The central bank respects market forces and the exchange rate is to determined by the market," it said.

Using unusually frank language, the central bank said southeast Asia's beleaguered currencies were "obviously overvalued" and that Taiwan's economy was very healthy -- and thus different from those in southeast Asia.
The bank said many southeast Asian countries had low foreign exchange reserves, huge foreign debts and persistent deficits in their trade and current accounts.
"Their currencies are obviously overvalued. Our country's situation is different," it added.
Taiwan's central bank was conspicuously excluded from a gathering of the region's central bankers on Friday in Shanghai, where the region's currency woes was a top agenda topic.

Listing Taiwan's strong fundamentals, the central bank said first-quarter gross domestic product growth was 6.83 percent and second-quarter growth has been estimated at 5.61 percent -- putting Taiwan on track to achieve 6.24 growth for all of 1997.
Taiwan's trade surplus in the first half was US$3.5 billion, and the first-quarter current account registered a surplus of $1.9 billion, the bank said.
The island's jobless rate was 2.67 percent in June, with consumer price inflation at just 1.37 percent for the half of 1997, it added.
